revision.text:
[[ja:三島・大山祇信仰]] [[ja:三島・大山祇信仰]] [[ja:三島・大山祇信仰]] [[File:Ohyamazumi Shrine Haiden.JPG|270px|thumb|[[Ōyamazumi Shrine]]]] [[File:Mishima-taisha shaden.JPG|270px|thumb|[[Mishima Taisha]]]] The Mishima and Ōyamazumi faith ('''三島・大山祇信仰) is a Shinto faith centered on the two shrines [[Ōyamazumi Shrine]] and [[Mishima Taisha]] {{Cite book|和書|author=岡田莊司・加藤直弥|date=2007|publisher=國學院大|title=現代・神社の信仰分布|isbn=|pages=25-27}}'''. == Overview == This group of shrines is primarily represented by those called {{ill|Mishima Taisha|lt=Mishima Taisha|lt=Mishima Shrine|ja|三島神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mishima Shrine|qq=}} (also written as 三嶋神社) and {{ill|Ōyamazumi Shrine|en|Ōyamazumi Shrine|WD=Q703904|lt=Ōyamazumi Shrine}} (also written as 大山積神社). There are approximately 700 to 1,300Ōmishima Town History, "Ōyamazumi Shrine Edition" shrines with these names across Japan. They exist in 44 {{ill|Prefectures of Japan|en|Prefectures of Japan|WD=Q50337|lt=prefectures of Japan}}, ranging from {{ill|Hokkaido|en|Hokkaido|WD=Q35581|lt=Hokkaidō}} to {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture}}, though the densest concentration of worship is observed from {{ill|Western Shikoku|ja|西四国|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Western Shikoku|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 四国|1=Shikoku|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q13991}} to {{ill|Kyushu|en|Kyushu|WD=Q13987|lt=Kyūshū}}, as well as the periphery of the {{ill|Kantō region|en|Kantō region|WD=Q132480|lt=Kantō region}}, particularly in {{ill|Fukushima Prefecture|en|Fukushima Prefecture|WD=Q71707|lt=Fukushima Prefecture}}, {{ill|Niigata Prefecture|en|Niigata Prefecture|WD=Q132705|lt=Niigata Prefecture}}, and {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|en|Shizuoka Prefecture|WD=Q131320|lt=Shizuoka Prefecture}}. In {{ill|Ehime Prefecture|en|Ehime Prefecture|WD=Q123376|lt=Ehime Prefecture}}, where the Ōyamazumi Shrine on Ōmishima Island is located, the shrines are particularly concentrated, with over 100 Mishima Shrines alone. Within the prefecture, it is the most commonly worshiped shrine lineage{{Cite book |和書 |author=岡田莊司・加藤直弥 |date=2007 |publisher=國學院大 |title=現代・神社の信仰分布 |isbn= |pages=60 }}. Other regions with significant numbers include {{ill|Fukuoka Prefecture|en|Fukuoka Prefecture|WD=Q123258|lt=Fukuoka Prefecture}} and {{ill|Kōchi Prefecture|en|Kōchi Prefecture|WD=Q134093|lt=Kōchi Prefecture}}. The {{ill|Ōyamatsumi|en|Ōyamatsumi|WD=Q386563|lt=Ōyamatsumi}} deity, historically regarded as a Mishima deity, was originally a god of mountains. However, since Ōyamazumi Shrine is situated on the island of {{ill|Ōmishima Island|en|Ōmishima Island|WD=Q9009869|lt=Ōmishima}}, and {{ill|Mishima Taisha|en|Mishima Taisha|WD=Q650772|lt=Mishima Taisha}} was once believed to have been located in the {{ill|Izu Islands|en|Izu Islands|WD=Q864302|lt=Izu Islands}}, the Mishima deity has strong associations with maritime protection and island creation. From the mid-{{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}, the shrine gained the reverence of the {{ill|Kōno clan|ja|河野氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōno clan|qq=}} and the {{ill|Minamoto clan|en|Minamoto clan|WD=Q599881|lt=Genji}}, among other warrior families, and became well known as a god of war. The {{ill|Azuma Kagami|en|Azuma Kagami|WD=Q1042324|lt=Azuma Kagami}} records that {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|en|Minamoto no Yoritomo|WD=Q242800|lt=Minamoto no Yoritomo}} prayed at Mishima Taisha before raising his army‘Azuma Kagami’, Jishō 4 (治承四年) August 17. Additionally, 40% of the {{ill|National Treasure (Japan)|en|National Treasure (Japan)|WD=Q1139795|lt=National Treasures of Japan}} and {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|en|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|WD=Q1188622|lt=Important Cultural Property}} classified as weapons and armor are housed at the Ōyamazumi Shrine on Ōmishima. The deity was also worshipped as an agricultural god, with many records of rainmaking rituals. The Mishima Shrines across Japan can generally be classified into two major lineages based on their origin: the Iyo lineage and the Izu lineage. However, the categorization is not rigid, as some shrines have ancient origins, others claim descent from both lineages, and some perceive both shrines as the same deity. Until the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji period}}, Mishima Taisha was considered to be derived from the Ōyamazumi Shrine on Ōmishima, and they mutually influenced each other. The {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period}} text *Haruno no Miyamaji* (春の深山路) describes both shrines as regarding each other as their main shrine*Haruno no Miyamaji*, November 24. As of 2023, Ōyamazumi Shrine on Ōmishima enshrines {{ill|Ōyamazumi|ja|大山積神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōyamazumi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to オオヤマツミ|1=Ōyamatsumi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q386563}}[http://ehime-jinjacho.jp/jinja/?p=1542 Ehime Prefecture Shrine Association - Ōyamazumi Shrine], while Mishima Taisha, after undergoing another change in enshrined deities, now venerates both Ōyamazumi and {{ill|Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|lt=Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|lt=Kotoshironushi|ja|事代主神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotoshironushi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 事代主}}, collectively worshiped as {{ill|Mishima Daimyōjin|ja|三島大明神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mishima Daimyōjin|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 三島・大山祇信仰|1=Mishima–Ōyamazumi cult|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q127948103}} or the Mishima deity[https://www.mishimataisha.or.jp/shrine Mishima Taisha Official Site]. == Worshipped Deities (Saijin) == {{see also|{{ill|Saijin|ja|祭神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saijin|qq=}}}} The current {{ill|Enshrined Deities|ja|祭神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Enshrined Deities|1=saijin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11591100}} are as follows: at Daisan‐shima’s Ōyamatsumi Shrine, the deity {{ill|Ōyamatsumi|en|Ōyamatsumi|WD=Q386563|lt=Ōyamatsumi}}; at Mishima Taisha, the deities are Ōyamatsumi (大山祇命) and {{ill|Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|lt=Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|lt=Kotoshironushi|ja|事代主神|lt=Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|lt=Kotoshironushi|lt_ja=積羽八重事代主神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotoshironushi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 事代主}}. In Ōyamatsumi Shrines such as {{ill|Ōyamatsumi Shrine (disambiguation)|ja|大山祇神社 (曖昧さ回避)|lt=Ōyamatsumi Shrine|lt_ja=大山祇神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōyamatsumi Shrine (disambiguation)|1=Ōyamazumi Shrine (disambiguation)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q16278443}} and in the Iyo lineage of Mishima Shrines the deity Ōyamatsumi is venerated, while in the Izu lineage of Mishima Shrines either Ōyamatsumi or Kotoshironushi is enshrined singly or both are enshrined together. Besides the names Ōyamatsumi (命) and Ōyamatsumi (命), variants such as Ōyamatsumi Tsumi, Ōyamatsumi Sumino, and Ōyamatsumi Tsutsumi are also attested. In both Mishima Taisha and the Izu lineage of Mishima Shrines, it is recorded that before the Edo period the enshrined deity was Ōyamatsumi (命), and it was only after the Meiji period that Kotoshironushi came to be enshrined. This change has not been without criticism{{Cite book|和書|editor=教部省|author=|year=1925|title={{ill|Selected Divine Names List|ja|特選神名牒|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Selected Divine Names List|1=Tokusen Jinmyōchō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11571092}}|publisher=磯部甲陽堂|page=299p|isbn=|ref=}}; at Mishima Taisha, in {{ill|1952|en|1952|WD=Q5272|lt=1952}}, the two deities Ōyamatsumi and Kotoshironushi were collectively re-designated and enshrined as either “Mishima Daimyōjin” or “Mishima Shrine.” For details on the post-Meiji changes in the enshrined deities at Mishima Taisha, see {{ill|Mishima Taisha#About the enshrined deities|ja|三嶋大社#祭神について|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mishima Taisha#About the enshrined deities|qq=}}. There are various theories regarding the identity of the Mishima deity. In addition to the Ōyamatsumi theory and the Kotoshironushi theory, there exist theories equating this deity with that of {{ill|Kamo shrines|en|Kamo shrines|WD=Q1306606|lt=Kamo Shrine}}Kitabatake Chikafusa, 『二十一社記』 賀茂社ノ条 or positing a deity of the {{ill|Izu Islands|en|Izu Islands|WD=Q864302|lt=Izu Islands}}.{{Cite book|和書|editor=|author=|year=1943|title=伊古奈比咩命神社|publisher=伊古奈比咩命神社|page=24|isbn=|ref=}} According to one interpretation, the Mishima deity of Iyo – originally venerated as Ōyamatsumi in Iyo – was combined through syncretism ({{ill|Religious syncretism|en|Religious syncretism|WD=Q21652002|lt=Syncretism}}) with the Watashi Ōkami from Settsu ({{ill|Settsu Province|en|Settsu Province|WD=Q864163|lt=Settsu}}) to form the Iyo Mishima deity. Another theory holds that the deity of the Izu Islands, regarded as Ōyamatsumi, after being transferred to the Mishima region later merged with a local water deity to form the Izu Mishima deity.日本の神社大全5 甲信/東海1 Among the representative descriptions found in pre‐medieval literature are the following: * In the 『Iyo Fudoki』 – the deity of Mishima (Mishima/Onshima) is identified as Ōyamatsumi. * In the {{ill|Engishiki Divine Name List|ja|延喜式神名帳|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki Divine Name List|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki Jinmyōchō|qq=}} – in Ochi District of Iyo Province, the great divine shrine “Ōyamatsumi Shrine” is listed (with Mishima Taisha appearing under the name “Izu Mishima Shrine”). * In {{ill|Tōkan Kikō|ja|東関紀行|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tōkan Kikō|1=Tōkan Kikō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11528660}}, {{ill|Genpei Jōsuiki|en|Genpei Jōsuiki|WD=Q3020148|lt=Genpei Seisui-ki}}, and {{ill|Shintōshū|en|Shintōshū|WD=Q2616931|lt=Shintōshū}} – the Izu Mishima deity is said to have come from Iyo. * In the 『Record of the Twenty-One Shrines』 and 『Deep Mountain Path in Spring』 – the Iyo and Izu Mishima deities are treated as identical. * In {{ill|Shaku Nihongi|en|Shaku Nihongi|WD=Q2710483|lt=Shaku Nihonki}}, {{ill|Nihon Shoki Sanso|ja|日本書紀纂疏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nihon Shoki Sanso|1=Nihon Shoki Sanso|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11508272}}, and {{ill|The Record of Japan's First Shrines|ja|大日本国一宮記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/The Record of Japan's First Shrines|1=Dai Nippon Koku Ichinomiya Ki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11435648}} – the Iyo and Izu Mishima deities are identified as Ōyamatsumi. * In the 『Record of the Twenty-Two Shrines Original Relations』 – the Iyo and Izu Mishima deities are identified as Kotoshironushi (this is cited as the basis for the Kotoshironushi theory; however, it is considered a misprint made during the transcription of the underlying 『Record of the Twenty-One Shrines』{{Cite book|和書|editor=|author=三島通良|year=1917|chapter=|title=伊豆国史蹟研究第一報書摘要|publisher=|isbn=|ref=}}). == History == For the founding legends of {{ill|Ōyamazumi Shrine|en|Ōyamazumi Shrine|WD=Q703904|lt=Ōyamazumi Shrine}} and {{ill|Mishima Taisha|en|Mishima Taisha|WD=Q650772|lt=Mishima Taisha}}, see their respective articles. Although both shrines have traditions of relocation (transference of the enshrined deity), both are generally negative about such transfers[https://oomishimagu.jp/about/ Ōyamatsumi Shrine – About][https://www.mishimataisha.or.jp/shrine Mishima Taisha History]. Excluding shrine legends, the earliest appearance of the deities in historical sources is found in the 『Shinshō Kakutoku Fushō』 (completed in 806), which records that in 758 the Izu Mishima deity was conferred a formal Rank. The 『Iyo Fudoki』 (believed to have been compiled by 748) also contains a passage stating that the deity of Mishima (Onshima) is Ōyamatsumi; however, the Fudoki itself has been lost and survives only as an excerpt quoted in the late Kamakura-period {{ill|Shaku Nihongi|en|Shaku Nihongi|WD=Q2710483|lt=Shaku Nihonki}}. The lost work 『Izu Kokufudoki』, too, contains no reference to the Izu Mishima deity in its scant surviving fragments. According to the 『Tango Kyūjiki』, it seems that the lost {{ill|Tango Kokufudoki|ja|丹後国風土記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tango Kokufudoki|1=Tango no Kuni Fudoki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11368517}} once mentioned {{ill|Mishimada Shrine|ja|三嶋田神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mishimada Shrine|1=Mishimada Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q131924351}}, but that work is also no longer extant. In other Heian-period sources, the place-name “Mishima” appears frequently – for example, it is first attested in {{ill|Wamyō Ruijushō|ja|倭名類聚抄|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wamyō Ruijushō|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 和名類聚抄}}. Several waka anthologies include poems about the Mishima deity; the Jitsukata-shū includes a poem on “mishima no kami”（Whether referring to Iyo or Settsu is unclear – 新日本古典文学大系）, and both the {{ill|Nōinshū|ja|能因集|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nōinshū|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} and {{ill|Kin'yō Wakashū|en|Kin'yō Wakashū|WD=Q1143249|lt=Konaha Wakashū}} contain poems about the Iyo Mishima deity (of Ōyamatsumi Shrine). The {{ill|Goshūi Wakashū|en|Goshūi Wakashū|WD=Q115108|lt=Goshūi Wakashū}} also includes a poem about the Eastern Journey ({{ill|Eastern Journey|ja|東遊|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Eastern Journey|1=Azuma Asobi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11528414}}) of the Iyo Mishima Myōjin. The tales of the Iyo Mishima deity are likewise recounted in the {{ill|Shunrai Zuinō|ja|俊頼髄脳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shunrai Zuinō|1=Toshiyori Zuinō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11385629}} and the {{ill|Ōkagami|en|Ōkagami|WD=Q385120|lt=Ōkagami}}. === Six Provinces History === In the Six Provinces History, three shrines are noted: Ōyamatsumi Shrine, Izu Mishima Shrine, and Mishima Kamo Shrine. Of these, the Ōyamatsumi Shrine of Iyo Province was successively promoted after being awarded the Junior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade (in {{ill|Shoku Nihongi|en|Shoku Nihongi|WD=Q611399|lt=Shoku Nihonki}}) in {{ill|766|en|766|WD=Q30564|lt=766}}, reaching the Senior Second Rank by 875 ({{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|en|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|WD=Q1052981|lt=The Three Generations of Japan: Official Records}}). The Izu Mishima deity is said to have manifested wondrous phenomena in 832, and as a result came to be regarded as a famous deity. However, the account in {{ill|Nihon Kōki|en|Nihon Kōki|WD=Q1077029|lt=Nihon Kōki}} (which covers the period 792–833) survives only in fragments quoted in {{ill|Shaku Nihongi|en|Shaku Nihongi|WD=Q2710483|lt=Shaku Nihonki}}, and it is presumed that a conferment of the Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade occurred around that time. In 850, the deity was awarded the Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade ({{ill|Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku|en|Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku|WD=Q1052905|lt=Nihon Buntoku Tennō Jitsuroku}}), and within a short period its divine Rank rapidly increased to the Junior Third Rank by 868 ({{ill|Ruijū Kokushi|en|Ruijū Kokushi|WD=Q1038639|lt=Ruiju Kokushi}}). In 884, the Mishima deity of Settsu Province was also awarded the Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade ({{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|en|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|WD=Q1052981|lt=The Three Generations of Japan: Official Records}}). After the period covered by the Six Provinces History, it is stated that Ōyamatsumi Shrine reached its Senior First Rank in {{ill|897|en|897|WD=Q30468|lt=897}}, and Izu Mishima Shrine reached the Senior First Rank by 1343, as recorded in the {{ill|Izu Province Divine Rank Register|ja|伊豆国神階帳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izu Province Divine Rank Register|1=Izu Province Divine Rank Register|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17193087}}. === Engishiki Divine Name List === The {{ill|Engishiki Divine Name List|ja|延喜式神名帳|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki Divine Name List|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki Jinmyōchō|qq=}}, completed in 927, records the following: * In Iyo Province’s Ochi District, the renowned divine shrine “Ōyamatsumi Shrine” (literally, “Ōyamatsumi Shrine”) – currently identified with the Ōyamatsumi Shrine of Daisan-shima. * In Izu Province’s Kamo District, the renowned divine shrine “Izu Mishima Shrine” – which is considered to be the predecessor of {{ill|Mishima Taisha|en|Mishima Taisha|WD=Q650772|lt=Mishima Taisha}}, though not identical; theories of transference or the enshrinement of a new shrine have been proposed. * In Echigo Province’s Kariwa District (displayed as “Mishima District”), the “Mishima Shrine” – which is regarded as the Mishima Shrine of Kashiwazaki City, though a transference theory exists.
(Here, {{ill|Kariwa District, Niigata|en|Kariwa District, Niigata|WD=Q1155110|lt=Mishima District}} is used to show the displayed name.) * In Tango Province’s Kumano District, the “Mishima-da Shrine” – currently represented by {{ill|Mishimada Shrine|ja|三嶋田神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mishimada Shrine|1=Mishimada Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q131924351}}. * In Settsu Province’s Shimogyo District, the “Mishima Kamo Shrine” – which is identified either with {{ill|Kamo Shrine (Takatsuki City)|ja|鴨神社 (高槻市)|lt=Kamo shrines|lt=Kamo Shrine|lt_ja=鴨神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamo Shrine (Takatsuki City)|1=Kamo Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11675604}} or with {{ill|Mishima Kamo Shrine|ja|三島鴨神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mishima Kamo Shrine|1=Mishima-Kamo Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11355295}}. In addition, a shrine known as Minishima Shrine in Takashima District of Ōmi Province – currently identified as {{ill|Minishima Shrine|ja|箕島神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Minishima Shrine|1=Mishima Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q134888252}} – is also considered to be part of the Mishima/Ōyamatsumi faith. == Shrines of Mishima and Ōyamatsumi Faith == When the principal shrine is taken to be the Ōyamatsumi Shrine of Daisan-shima ({{ill|Ōmishima Island|en|Ōmishima Island|WD=Q9009869|lt=Daisan-shima}}) and its Ōyamatsumi Shrine, the shrines are usually named “Mishima Shrine” or “Ōyamatsumi Shrine,” whereas when Mishima Taisha ({{ill|Mishima Taisha|en|Mishima Taisha|WD=Q650772|lt=Mishima Taisha}}) is regarded as the head shrine, the name “Mishima Shrine” is typically used. However, there are many exceptions and no fully systematized pattern. There are roughly 400 Mishima Shrines nationwide – approximately 111 in Ehime Prefecture and 36 in {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|en|Shizuoka Prefecture|WD=Q131320|lt=Shizuoka Prefecture}}, among others. Similarly, Ōyamatsumi Shrines are said to number between 293 and 897『大三島宮』1973rd year 1月。大三島大社講, or even up to 960, with 43 in {{ill|Fukuoka Prefecture|en|Fukuoka Prefecture|WD=Q123258|lt=Fukuoka Prefecture}} and 36 in {{ill|Fukushima Prefecture|en|Fukushima Prefecture|WD=Q71707|lt=Fukushima Prefecture}}, among others. Other related shrine names include Yama Shrines, numbering 78 (in {{ill|Kōchi Prefecture|en|Kōchi Prefecture|WD=Q134093|lt=Kōchi Prefecture}}, {{ill|Nagasaki Prefecture|en|Nagasaki Prefecture|WD=Q169376|lt=Nagasaki Prefecture}}, Fukuoka Prefecture, etc.), and Ōyama Shrines, numbering 42 (in {{ill|Hiroshima Prefecture|en|Hiroshima Prefecture|WD=Q617375|lt=Hiroshima Prefecture}}, Kōchi Prefecture, {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|en|Shimane Prefecture|WD=Q132751|lt=Shimane Prefecture}}, etc.), as well as Yamazumi Shrines, with 7 in (for example, {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|en|Shizuoka Prefecture|WD=Q131320|lt=Shizuoka Prefecture}}, etc.). In addition to these, shrines where Ōyamatsumi is the principal enshrined deity include, for example, the {{ill|Yama Shrine|ja|山神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yama Shrine|1=Mountain Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11470798}} (numbering 1,133), among others. Furthermore, when including subsidiary halls and sub-shrines within the precincts, the total number of shrines that enshrine Ōyamatsumi in some form is said to reach between 7,000[https://kaken.nii.ac.jp/ja/report/KAKENHI-PROJECT-17K02270/17K022702019jisseki/ 祭神別神社分布図による諸信仰伝播の過程および背景の研究（2019th year ）] and 10,0001973rd year 1月『大三島宮』大三島大社講（大山祇神社）1972nd year 8月の神社本庁調査に依る, and these are, at least in formal terms, sometimes regarded as subordinate to the head shrine, Ōyamatsumi Shrine of Daisan-shima[https://kojiki.kokugakuin.ac.jp/shinmei/oyamatsuminokami/ 大山津見神](國學院大學神名データベース). However, this relationship is a formal one based solely on the enshrined deities; the actual connection to the Mishima/Ōyamatsumi faith varies considerably – for example, the group of 438 shrines that enshrine Ōyamatsumi as one of twelve deities (the “Twelve-Shrine Faith”) is only loosely related, whereas the faith centered on the Asama Shrine (397 shrines), which frequently distributes Ōyamatsumi, is based on a parent–child relationship between the Mishima and Asama deities権 東祐「神話解釈史から見る富士山の祭神変貌論」『日本研究』（2023rd year 12月16日) {{doi|10.15055/00006788}}. === Major Shrines === ;Headquarters * [[ja:三島・大山祇信仰]] [[ja:三島・大山祇信仰]] [[ja:三島・大山祇信仰]] [[File:Ohyamazumi Shrine Haiden.JPG|270px|thumb|[[Ōyamazumi Shrine]]]] [[File:Mishima-taisha shaden.JPG|270px|thumb|[[Mishima Taisha]]]] The Mishima and Ōyamazumi faith ('''三島・大山祇信仰) is a Shinto faith centered on the two shrines [[Ōyamazumi Shrine]] and [[Mishima Taisha]] {{Cite book|和書|author=岡田莊司・加藤直弥|date=2007|publisher=國學院大|title=現代・神社の信仰分布|isbn=|pages=25-27}}'''. == Overview == This group of shrines is primarily represented by those called {{ill|Mishima Taisha|lt=Mishima Taisha|lt=Mishima Shrine|ja|三島神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mishima Shrine|qq=}} (also written as 三嶋神社) and {{ill|Ōyamazumi Shrine|en|Ōyamazumi Shrine|WD=Q703904|lt=Ōyamazumi Shrine}} (also written as 大山積神社). There are approximately 700 to 1,300Ōmishima Town History, "Ōyamazumi Shrine Edition" shrines with these names across Japan. They exist in 44 {{ill|Prefectures of Japan|en|Prefectures of Japan|WD=Q50337|lt=prefectures of Japan}}, ranging from {{ill|Hokkaido|en|Hokkaido|WD=Q35581|lt=Hokkaidō}} to {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture}}, though the densest concentration of worship is observed from {{ill|Western Shikoku|ja|西四国|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Western Shikoku|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 四国|1=Shikoku|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q13991}} to {{ill|Kyushu|en|Kyushu|WD=Q13987|lt=Kyūshū}}, as well as the periphery of the {{ill|Kantō region|en|Kantō region|WD=Q132480|lt=Kantō region}}, particularly in {{ill|Fukushima Prefecture|en|Fukushima Prefecture|WD=Q71707|lt=Fukushima Prefecture}}, {{ill|Niigata Prefecture|en|Niigata Prefecture|WD=Q132705|lt=Niigata Prefecture}}, and {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|en|Shizuoka Prefecture|WD=Q131320|lt=Shizuoka Prefecture}}. In {{ill|Ehime Prefecture|en|Ehime Prefecture|WD=Q123376|lt=Ehime Prefecture}}, where the Ōyamazumi Shrine on Ōmishima Island is located, the shrines are particularly concentrated, with over 100 Mishima Shrines alone. Within the prefecture, it is the most commonly worshiped shrine lineage{{Cite book |和書 |author=岡田莊司・加藤直弥 |date=2007 |publisher=國學院大 |title=現代・神社の信仰分布 |isbn= |pages=60 }}. Other regions with significant numbers include {{ill|Fukuoka Prefecture|en|Fukuoka Prefecture|WD=Q123258|lt=Fukuoka Prefecture}} and {{ill|Kōchi Prefecture|en|Kōchi Prefecture|WD=Q134093|lt=Kōchi Prefecture}}. The {{ill|Ōyamatsumi|en|Ōyamatsumi|WD=Q386563|lt=Ōyamatsumi}} deity, historically regarded as a Mishima deity, was originally a god of mountains. However, since Ōyamazumi Shrine is situated on the island of {{ill|Ōmishima Island|en|Ōmishima Island|WD=Q9009869|lt=Ōmishima}}, and {{ill|Mishima Taisha|en|Mishima Taisha|WD=Q650772|lt=Mishima Taisha}} was once believed to have been located in the {{ill|Izu Islands|en|Izu Islands|WD=Q864302|lt=Izu Islands}}, the Mishima deity has strong associations with maritime protection and island creation. From the mid-{{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}, the shrine gained the reverence of the {{ill|Kōno clan|ja|河野氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōno clan|qq=}} and the {{ill|Minamoto clan|en|Minamoto clan|WD=Q599881|lt=Genji}}, among other warrior families, and became well known as a god of war. The {{ill|Azuma Kagami|en|Azuma Kagami|WD=Q1042324|lt=Azuma Kagami}} records that {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|en|Minamoto no Yoritomo|WD=Q242800|lt=Minamoto no Yoritomo}} prayed at Mishima Taisha before raising his army‘Azuma Kagami’, Jishō 4 (治承四年) August 17. Additionally, 40% of the {{ill|National Treasure (Japan)|en|National Treasure (Japan)|WD=Q1139795|lt=National Treasures of Japan}} and {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|en|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|WD=Q1188622|lt=Important Cultural Property}} classified as weapons and armor are housed at the Ōyamazumi Shrine on Ōmishima. The deity was also worshipped as an agricultural god, with many records of rainmaking rituals. The Mishima Shrines across Japan can generally be classified into two major lineages based on their origin: the Iyo lineage and the Izu lineage. However, the categorization is not rigid, as some shrines have ancient origins, others claim descent from both lineages, and some perceive both shrines as the same deity. Until the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji period}}, Mishima Taisha was considered to be derived from the Ōyamazumi Shrine on Ōmishima, and they mutually influenced each other. The {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period}} text *Haruno no Miyamaji* (春の深山路) describes both shrines as regarding each other as their main shrine*Haruno no Miyamaji*, November 24. As of 2023, Ōyamazumi Shrine on Ōmishima enshrines {{ill|Ōyamazumi|ja|大山積神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōyamazumi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to オオヤマツミ|1=Ōyamatsumi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q386563}}[http://ehime-jinjacho.jp/jinja/?p=1542 Ehime Prefecture Shrine Association - Ōyamazumi Shrine], while Mishima Taisha, after undergoing another change in enshrined deities, now venerates both Ōyamazumi and {{ill|Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|WD=Q8009611|lt=Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|WD=Q8009611|lt=Kotoshironushi|ja|事代主神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotoshironushi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 事代主}}, collectively worshiped as {{ill|Mishima Daimyōjin|ja|三島大明神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mishima Daimyōjin|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 三島・大山祇信仰|1=Mishima–Ōyamazumi cult|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q127948103}} or the Mishima deity[https://www.mishimataisha.or.jp/shrine Mishima Taisha Official Site]. == Worshipped Deities (Saijin) == {{see also|{{ill|Saijin|ja|祭神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saijin|qq=}}}} The current {{ill|Enshrined Deities|ja|祭神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Enshrined Deities|1=saijin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11591100}} are as follows: at Daisan‐shima’s Ōyamatsumi Shrine, the deity {{ill|Ōyamatsumi|en|Ōyamatsumi|WD=Q386563|lt=Ōyamatsumi}}; at Mishima Taisha, the deities are Ōyamatsumi (大山祇命) and {{ill|Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|WD=Q8009611|lt=Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|WD=Q8009611|lt=Kotoshironushi|ja|事代主神|WD=Q8009611|lt=Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|WD=Q8009611|lt=Kotoshironushi|lt_ja=積羽八重事代主神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotoshironushi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 事代主}}. In Ōyamatsumi Shrines such as {{ill|Ōyamatsumi Shrine (disambiguation)|ja|大山祇神社 (曖昧さ回避)|lt=Ōyamatsumi Shrine|lt_ja=大山祇神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōyamatsumi Shrine (disambiguation)|1=Ōyamazumi Shrine (disambiguation)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q16278443}} and in the Iyo lineage of Mishima Shrines the deity Ōyamatsumi is venerated, while in the Izu lineage of Mishima Shrines either Ōyamatsumi or Kotoshironushi is enshrined singly or both are enshrined together. Besides the names Ōyamatsumi (命) and Ōyamatsumi (命), variants such as Ōyamatsumi Tsumi, Ōyamatsumi Sumino, and Ōyamatsumi Tsutsumi are also attested. In both Mishima Taisha and the Izu lineage of Mishima Shrines, it is recorded that before the Edo period the enshrined deity was Ōyamatsumi (命), and it was only after the Meiji period that Kotoshironushi came to be enshrined. This change has not been without criticism{{Cite book|和書|editor=教部省|author=|year=1925|title={{ill|Selected Divine Names List|ja|特選神名牒|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Selected Divine Names List|1=Tokusen Jinmyōchō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11571092}}|publisher=磯部甲陽堂|page=299p|isbn=|ref=}}; at Mishima Taisha, in {{ill|1952|en|1952|WD=Q5272|lt=1952}}, the two deities Ōyamatsumi and Kotoshironushi were collectively re-designated and enshrined as either “Mishima Daimyōjin” or “Mishima Shrine.” For details on the post-Meiji changes in the enshrined deities at Mishima Taisha, see {{ill|Mishima Taisha#About the enshrined deities|ja|三嶋大社#祭神について|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mishima Taisha#About the enshrined deities|qq=}}. There are various theories regarding the identity of the Mishima deity. In addition to the Ōyamatsumi theory and the Kotoshironushi theory, there exist theories equating this deity with that of {{ill|Kamo shrines|en|Kamo shrines|WD=Q1306606|lt=Kamo Shrine}}Kitabatake Chikafusa, 『二十一社記』 賀茂社ノ条 or positing a deity of the {{ill|Izu Islands|en|Izu Islands|WD=Q864302|lt=Izu Islands}}.{{Cite book|和書|editor=|author=|year=1943|title=伊古奈比咩命神社|publisher=伊古奈比咩命神社|page=24|isbn=|ref=}} According to one interpretation, the Mishima deity of Iyo – originally venerated as Ōyamatsumi in Iyo – was combined through syncretism ({{ill|Religious syncretism|en|Religious syncretism|WD=Q21652002|lt=Syncretism}}) with the Watashi Ōkami from Settsu ({{ill|Settsu Province|en|Settsu Province|WD=Q864163|lt=Settsu}}) to form the Iyo Mishima deity. Another theory holds that the deity of the Izu Islands, regarded as Ōyamatsumi, after being transferred to the Mishima region later merged with a local water deity to form the Izu Mishima deity.日本の神社大全5 甲信/東海1 Among the representative descriptions found in pre‐medieval literature are the following: * In the 『Iyo Fudoki』 – the deity of Mishima (Mishima/Onshima) is identified as Ōyamatsumi. * In the {{ill|Engishiki Divine Name List|ja|延喜式神名帳|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki Divine Name List|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki Jinmyōchō|qq=}} – in Ochi District of Iyo Province, the great divine shrine “Ōyamatsumi Shrine” is listed (with Mishima Taisha appearing under the name “Izu Mishima Shrine”). * In {{ill|Tōkan Kikō|ja|東関紀行|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tōkan Kikō|1=Tōkan Kikō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11528660}}, {{ill|Genpei Jōsuiki|en|Genpei Jōsuiki|WD=Q3020148|lt=Genpei Seisui-ki}}, and {{ill|Shintōshū|en|Shintōshū|WD=Q2616931|lt=Shintōshū}} – the Izu Mishima deity is said to have come from Iyo. * In the 『Record of the Twenty-One Shrines』 and 『Deep Mountain Path in Spring』 – the Iyo and Izu Mishima deities are treated as identical. * In {{ill|Shaku Nihongi|en|Shaku Nihongi|WD=Q2710483|lt=Shaku Nihonki}}, {{ill|Nihon Shoki Sanso|ja|日本書紀纂疏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nihon Shoki Sanso|1=Nihon Shoki Sanso|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11508272}}, and {{ill|The Record of Japan's First Shrines|ja|大日本国一宮記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/The Record of Japan's First Shrines|1=Dai Nippon Koku Ichinomiya Ki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11435648}} – the Iyo and Izu Mishima deities are identified as Ōyamatsumi. * In the 『Record of the Twenty-Two Shrines Original Relations』 – the Iyo and Izu Mishima deities are identified as Kotoshironushi (this is cited as the basis for the Kotoshironushi theory; however, it is considered a misprint made during the transcription of the underlying 『Record of the Twenty-One Shrines』{{Cite book|和書|editor=|author=三島通良|year=1917|chapter=|title=伊豆国史蹟研究第一報書摘要|publisher=|isbn=|ref=}}). == History == For the founding legends of {{ill|Ōyamazumi Shrine|en|Ōyamazumi Shrine|WD=Q703904|lt=Ōyamazumi Shrine}} and {{ill|Mishima Taisha|en|Mishima Taisha|WD=Q650772|lt=Mishima Taisha}}, see their respective articles. Although both shrines have traditions of relocation (transference of the enshrined deity), both are generally negative about such transfers[https://oomishimagu.jp/about/ Ōyamatsumi Shrine – About][https://www.mishimataisha.or.jp/shrine Mishima Taisha History]. Excluding shrine legends, the earliest appearance of the deities in historical sources is found in the 『Shinshō Kakutoku Fushō』 (completed in 806), which records that in 758 the Izu Mishima deity was conferred a formal Rank. The 『Iyo Fudoki』 (believed to have been compiled by 748) also contains a passage stating that the deity of Mishima (Onshima) is Ōyamatsumi; however, the Fudoki itself has been lost and survives only as an excerpt quoted in the late Kamakura-period {{ill|Shaku Nihongi|en|Shaku Nihongi|WD=Q2710483|lt=Shaku Nihonki}}. The lost work 『Izu Kokufudoki』, too, contains no reference to the Izu Mishima deity in its scant surviving fragments. According to the 『Tango Kyūjiki』, it seems that the lost {{ill|Tango Kokufudoki|ja|丹後国風土記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tango Kokufudoki|1=Tango no Kuni Fudoki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11368517}} once mentioned {{ill|Mishimada Shrine|ja|三嶋田神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mishimada Shrine|1=Mishimada Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q131924351}}, but that work is also no longer extant. In other Heian-period sources, the place-name “Mishima” appears frequently – for example, it is first attested in {{ill|Wamyō Ruijushō|ja|倭名類聚抄|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wamyō Ruijushō|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 和名類聚抄}}. Several waka anthologies include poems about the Mishima deity; the Jitsukata-shū includes a poem on “mishima no kami”（Whether referring to Iyo or Settsu is unclear – 新日本古典文学大系）, and both the {{ill|Nōinshū|ja|能因集|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nōinshū|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} and {{ill|Kin'yō Wakashū|en|Kin'yō Wakashū|WD=Q1143249|lt=Konaha Wakashū}} contain poems about the Iyo Mishima deity (of Ōyamatsumi Shrine). The {{ill|Goshūi Wakashū|en|Goshūi Wakashū|WD=Q115108|lt=Goshūi Wakashū}} also includes a poem about the Eastern Journey ({{ill|Eastern Journey|ja|東遊|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Eastern Journey|1=Azuma Asobi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11528414}}) of the Iyo Mishima Myōjin. The tales of the Iyo Mishima deity are likewise recounted in the {{ill|Shunrai Zuinō|ja|俊頼髄脳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shunrai Zuinō|1=Toshiyori Zuinō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11385629}} and the {{ill|Ōkagami|en|Ōkagami|WD=Q385120|lt=Ōkagami}}. === Six Provinces History === In the Six Provinces History, three shrines are noted: Ōyamatsumi Shrine, Izu Mishima Shrine, and Mishima Kamo Shrine. Of these, the Ōyamatsumi Shrine of Iyo Province was successively promoted after being awarded the Junior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade (in {{ill|Shoku Nihongi|en|Shoku Nihongi|WD=Q611399|lt=Shoku Nihonki}}) in {{ill|766|en|766|WD=Q30564|lt=766}}, reaching the Senior Second Rank by 875 ({{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|en|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|WD=Q1052981|lt=The Three Generations of Japan: Official Records}}). The Izu Mishima deity is said to have manifested wondrous phenomena in 832, and as a result came to be regarded as a famous deity. However, the account in {{ill|Nihon Kōki|en|Nihon Kōki|WD=Q1077029|lt=Nihon Kōki}} (which covers the period 792–833) survives only in fragments quoted in {{ill|Shaku Nihongi|en|Shaku Nihongi|WD=Q2710483|lt=Shaku Nihonki}}, and it is presumed that a conferment of the Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade occurred around that time. In 850, the deity was awarded the Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade ({{ill|Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku|en|Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku|WD=Q1052905|lt=Nihon Buntoku Tennō Jitsuroku}}), and within a short period its divine Rank rapidly increased to the Junior Third Rank by 868 ({{ill|Ruijū Kokushi|en|Ruijū Kokushi|WD=Q1038639|lt=Ruiju Kokushi}}). In 884, the Mishima deity of Settsu Province was also awarded the Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade ({{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|en|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|WD=Q1052981|lt=The Three Generations of Japan: Official Records}}). After the period covered by the Six Provinces History, it is stated that Ōyamatsumi Shrine reached its Senior First Rank in {{ill|897|en|897|WD=Q30468|lt=897}}, and Izu Mishima Shrine reached the Senior First Rank by 1343, as recorded in the {{ill|Izu Province Divine Rank Register|ja|伊豆国神階帳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izu Province Divine Rank Register|1=Izu Province Divine Rank Register|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17193087}}. === Engishiki Divine Name List === The {{ill|Engishiki Divine Name List|ja|延喜式神名帳|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki Divine Name List|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki Jinmyōchō|qq=}}, completed in 927, records the following: * In Iyo Province’s Ochi District, the renowned divine shrine “Ōyamatsumi Shrine” (literally, “Ōyamatsumi Shrine”) – currently identified with the Ōyamatsumi Shrine of Daisan-shima. * In Izu Province’s Kamo District, the renowned divine shrine “Izu Mishima Shrine” – which is considered to be the predecessor of {{ill|Mishima Taisha|en|Mishima Taisha|WD=Q650772|lt=Mishima Taisha}}, though not identical; theories of transference or the enshrinement of a new shrine have been proposed. * In Echigo Province’s Kariwa District (displayed as “Mishima District”), the “Mishima Shrine” – which is regarded as the Mishima Shrine of Kashiwazaki City, though a transference theory exists.
(Here, {{ill|Kariwa District, Niigata|en|Kariwa District, Niigata|WD=Q1155110|lt=Mishima District}} is used to show the displayed name.) * In Tango Province’s Kumano District, the “Mishima-da Shrine” – currently represented by {{ill|Mishimada Shrine|ja|三嶋田神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mishimada Shrine|1=Mishimada Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q131924351}}. * In Settsu Province’s Shimogyo District, the “Mishima Kamo Shrine” – which is identified either with {{ill|Kamo Shrine (Takatsuki City)|ja|鴨神社 (高槻市)|lt=Kamo shrines|lt=Kamo Shrine|lt_ja=鴨神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamo Shrine (Takatsuki City)|1=Kamo Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11675604}} or with {{ill|Mishima Kamo Shrine|ja|三島鴨神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mishima Kamo Shrine|1=Mishima-Kamo Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11355295}}. In addition, a shrine known as Minishima Shrine in Takashima District of Ōmi Province – currently identified as {{ill|Minishima Shrine|ja|箕島神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Minishima Shrine|1=Mishima Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q134888252}} – is also considered to be part of the Mishima/Ōyamatsumi faith. == Shrines of Mishima and Ōyamatsumi Faith == When the principal shrine is taken to be the Ōyamatsumi Shrine of Daisan-shima ({{ill|Ōmishima Island|en|Ōmishima Island|WD=Q9009869|lt=Daisan-shima}}) and its Ōyamatsumi Shrine, the shrines are usually named “Mishima Shrine” or “Ōyamatsumi Shrine,” whereas when Mishima Taisha ({{ill|Mishima Taisha|en|Mishima Taisha|WD=Q650772|lt=Mishima Taisha}}) is regarded as the head shrine, the name “Mishima Shrine” is typically used. However, there are many exceptions and no fully systematized pattern. There are roughly 400 Mishima Shrines nationwide – approximately 111 in Ehime Prefecture and 36 in {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|en|Shizuoka Prefecture|WD=Q131320|lt=Shizuoka Prefecture}}, among others. Similarly, Ōyamatsumi Shrines are said to number between 293 and 897『大三島宮』1973rd year 1月。大三島大社講, or even up to 960, with 43 in {{ill|Fukuoka Prefecture|en|Fukuoka Prefecture|WD=Q123258|lt=Fukuoka Prefecture}} and 36 in {{ill|Fukushima Prefecture|en|Fukushima Prefecture|WD=Q71707|lt=Fukushima Prefecture}}, among others. Other related shrine names include Yama Shrines, numbering 78 (in {{ill|Kōchi Prefecture|en|Kōchi Prefecture|WD=Q134093|lt=Kōchi Prefecture}}, {{ill|Nagasaki Prefecture|en|Nagasaki Prefecture|WD=Q169376|lt=Nagasaki Prefecture}}, Fukuoka Prefecture, etc.), and Ōyama Shrines, numbering 42 (in {{ill|Hiroshima Prefecture|en|Hiroshima Prefecture|WD=Q617375|lt=Hiroshima Prefecture}}, Kōchi Prefecture, {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|en|Shimane Prefecture|WD=Q132751|lt=Shimane Prefecture}}, etc.), as well as Yamazumi Shrines, with 7 in (for example, {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|en|Shizuoka Prefecture|WD=Q131320|lt=Shizuoka Prefecture}}, etc.). In addition to these, shrines where Ōyamatsumi is the principal enshrined deity include, for example, the {{ill|Yama Shrine|ja|山神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yama Shrine|1=Mountain Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11470798}} (numbering 1,133), among others. Furthermore, when including subsidiary halls and sub-shrines within the precincts, the total number of shrines that enshrine Ōyamatsumi in some form is said to reach between 7,000[https://kaken.nii.ac.jp/ja/report/KAKENHI-PROJECT-17K02270/17K022702019jisseki/ 祭神別神社分布図による諸信仰伝播の過程および背景の研究（2019th year ）] and 10,0001973rd year 1月『大三島宮』大三島大社講（大山祇神社）1972nd year 8月の神社本庁調査に依る, and these are, at least in formal terms, sometimes regarded as subordinate to the head shrine, Ōyamatsumi Shrine of Daisan-shima[https://kojiki.kokugakuin.ac.jp/shinmei/oyamatsuminokami/ 大山津見神](國學院大學神名データベース). However, this relationship is a formal one based solely on the enshrined deities; the actual connection to the Mishima/Ōyamatsumi faith varies considerably – for example, the group of 438 shrines that enshrine Ōyamatsumi as one of twelve deities (the “Twelve-Shrine Faith”) is only loosely related, whereas the faith centered on the Asama Shrine (397 shrines), which frequently distributes Ōyamatsumi, is based on a parent–child relationship between the Mishima and Asama deities権 東祐「神話解釈史から見る富士山の祭神変貌論」『日本研究』（2023rd year 12月16日) {{doi|10.15055/00006788}}. === Major Shrines === ;Headquarters * [[ja:三島・大山祇信仰]] [[ja:三島・大山祇信仰]] [[ja:三島・大山祇信仰]] [[File:Ohyamazumi Shrine Haiden.JPG|270px|thumb|[[Ōyamazumi Shrine]]]] [[File:Mishima-taisha shaden.JPG|270px|thumb|[[Mishima Taisha]]]] The Mishima and Ōyamazumi faith ('''三島・大山祇信仰) is a Shinto faith centered on the two shrines [[Ōyamazumi Shrine]] and [[Mishima Taisha]] {{Cite book|和書|author=岡田莊司・加藤直弥|date=2007|publisher=國學院大|title=現代・神社の信仰分布|isbn=|pages=25-27}}'''. == Overview == This group of shrines is primarily represented by those called {{ill|Mishima Taisha|lt=Mishima Taisha|lt=Mishima Shrine|ja|三島神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mishima Shrine|qq=}} (also written as 三嶋神社) and {{ill|Ōyamazumi Shrine|en|Ōyamazumi Shrine|WD=Q703904|lt=Ōyamazumi Shrine}} (also written as 大山積神社). There are approximately 700 to 1,300Ōmishima Town History, "Ōyamazumi Shrine Edition" shrines with these names across Japan. They exist in 44 {{ill|Prefectures of Japan|en|Prefectures of Japan|WD=Q50337|lt=prefectures of Japan}}, ranging from {{ill|Hokkaido|en|Hokkaido|WD=Q35581|lt=Hokkaidō}} to {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture}}, though the densest concentration of worship is observed from {{ill|Western Shikoku|ja|西四国|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Western Shikoku|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 四国|1=Shikoku|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q13991}} to {{ill|Kyushu|en|Kyushu|WD=Q13987|lt=Kyūshū}}, as well as the periphery of the {{ill|Kantō region|en|Kantō region|WD=Q132480|lt=Kantō region}}, particularly in {{ill|Fukushima Prefecture|en|Fukushima Prefecture|WD=Q71707|lt=Fukushima Prefecture}}, {{ill|Niigata Prefecture|en|Niigata Prefecture|WD=Q132705|lt=Niigata Prefecture}}, and {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|en|Shizuoka Prefecture|WD=Q131320|lt=Shizuoka Prefecture}}. In {{ill|Ehime Prefecture|en|Ehime Prefecture|WD=Q123376|lt=Ehime Prefecture}}, where the Ōyamazumi Shrine on Ōmishima Island is located, the shrines are particularly concentrated, with over 100 Mishima Shrines alone. Within the prefecture, it is the most commonly worshiped shrine lineage{{Cite book |和書 |author=岡田莊司・加藤直弥 |date=2007 |publisher=國學院大 |title=現代・神社の信仰分布 |isbn= |pages=60 }}. Other regions with significant numbers include {{ill|Fukuoka Prefecture|en|Fukuoka Prefecture|WD=Q123258|lt=Fukuoka Prefecture}} and {{ill|Kōchi Prefecture|en|Kōchi Prefecture|WD=Q134093|lt=Kōchi Prefecture}}. The {{ill|Ōyamatsumi|en|Ōyamatsumi|WD=Q386563|WD=Q386563|lt=Ōyamatsumi}} deity, historically regarded as a Mishima deity, was originally a god of mountains. However, since Ōyamazumi Shrine is situated on the island of {{ill|Ōmishima Island|en|Ōmishima Island|WD=Q9009869|lt=Ōmishima}}, and {{ill|Mishima Taisha|en|Mishima Taisha|WD=Q650772|lt=Mishima Taisha}} was once believed to have been located in the {{ill|Izu Islands|en|Izu Islands|WD=Q864302|lt=Izu Islands}}, the Mishima deity has strong associations with maritime protection and island creation. From the mid-{{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}, the shrine gained the reverence of the {{ill|Kōno clan|ja|河野氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōno clan|qq=}} and the {{ill|Minamoto clan|en|Minamoto clan|WD=Q599881|lt=Genji}}, among other warrior families, and became well known as a god of war. The {{ill|Azuma Kagami|en|Azuma Kagami|WD=Q1042324|lt=Azuma Kagami}} records that {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|en|Minamoto no Yoritomo|WD=Q242800|lt=Minamoto no Yoritomo}} prayed at Mishima Taisha before raising his army‘Azuma Kagami’, Jishō 4 (治承四年) August 17. Additionally, 40% of the {{ill|National Treasure (Japan)|en|National Treasure (Japan)|WD=Q1139795|lt=National Treasures of Japan}} and {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|en|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|WD=Q1188622|lt=Important Cultural Property}} classified as weapons and armor are housed at the Ōyamazumi Shrine on Ōmishima. The deity was also worshipped as an agricultural god, with many records of rainmaking rituals. The Mishima Shrines across Japan can generally be classified into two major lineages based on their origin: the Iyo lineage and the Izu lineage. However, the categorization is not rigid, as some shrines have ancient origins, others claim descent from both lineages, and some perceive both shrines as the same deity. Until the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji period}}, Mishima Taisha was considered to be derived from the Ōyamazumi Shrine on Ōmishima, and they mutually influenced each other. The {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period}} text *Haruno no Miyamaji* (春の深山路) describes both shrines as regarding each other as their main shrine*Haruno no Miyamaji*, November 24. As of 2023, Ōyamazumi Shrine on Ōmishima enshrines {{ill|Ōyamazumi|ja|大山積神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōyamazumi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to オオヤマツミ|1=Ōyamatsumi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q386563}}[http://ehime-jinjacho.jp/jinja/?p=1542 Ehime Prefecture Shrine Association - Ōyamazumi Shrine], while Mishima Taisha, after undergoing another change in enshrined deities, now venerates both Ōyamazumi and {{ill|Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|WD=Q8009611|lt=Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|WD=Q8009611|lt=Kotoshironushi|ja|事代主神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotoshironushi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 事代主}}, collectively worshiped as {{ill|Mishima Daimyōjin|ja|三島大明神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mishima Daimyōjin|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 三島・大山祇信仰|1=Mishima–Ōyamazumi cult|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q127948103}} or the Mishima deity[https://www.mishimataisha.or.jp/shrine Mishima Taisha Official Site]. == Worshipped Deities (Saijin) == {{see also|{{ill|Saijin|ja|祭神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saijin|qq=}}}} The current {{ill|Enshrined Deities|ja|祭神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Enshrined Deities|1=saijin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11591100}} are as follows: at Daisan‐shima’s Ōyamatsumi Shrine, the deity {{ill|Ōyamatsumi|en|Ōyamatsumi|WD=Q386563|WD=Q386563|lt=Ōyamatsumi}}; at Mishima Taisha, the deities are Ōyamatsumi (大山祇命) and {{ill|Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|WD=Q8009611|lt=Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|WD=Q8009611|lt=Kotoshironushi|ja|事代主神|WD=Q8009611|lt=Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|WD=Q8009611|lt=Kotoshironushi|lt_ja=積羽八重事代主神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotoshironushi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 事代主}}. In Ōyamatsumi Shrines such as {{ill|Ōyamatsumi Shrine (disambiguation)|ja|大山祇神社 (曖昧さ回避)|WD=Q386563|lt=Ōyamatsumi Shrine|lt_ja=大山祇神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōyamatsumi Shrine (disambiguation)|1=Ōyamazumi Shrine (disambiguation)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q16278443}} and in the Iyo lineage of Mishima Shrines the deity Ōyamatsumi is venerated, while in the Izu lineage of Mishima Shrines either Ōyamatsumi or Kotoshironushi is enshrined singly or both are enshrined together. Besides the names Ōyamatsumi (命) and Ōyamatsumi (命), variants such as Ōyamatsumi Tsumi, Ōyamatsumi Sumino, and Ōyamatsumi Tsutsumi are also attested. In both Mishima Taisha and the Izu lineage of Mishima Shrines, it is recorded that before the Edo period the enshrined deity was Ōyamatsumi (命), and it was only after the Meiji period that Kotoshironushi came to be enshrined. This change has not been without criticism{{Cite book|和書|editor=教部省|author=|year=1925|title={{ill|Selected Divine Names List|ja|特選神名牒|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Selected Divine Names List|1=Tokusen Jinmyōchō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11571092}}|publisher=磯部甲陽堂|page=299p|isbn=|ref=}}; at Mishima Taisha, in {{ill|1952|en|1952|WD=Q5272|lt=1952}}, the two deities Ōyamatsumi and Kotoshironushi were collectively re-designated and enshrined as either “Mishima Daimyōjin” or “Mishima Shrine.” For details on the post-Meiji changes in the enshrined deities at Mishima Taisha, see {{ill|Mishima Taisha#About the enshrined deities|ja|三嶋大社#祭神について|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mishima Taisha#About the enshrined deities|qq=}}. There are various theories regarding the identity of the Mishima deity. In addition to the Ōyamatsumi theory and the Kotoshironushi theory, there exist theories equating this deity with that of {{ill|Kamo shrines|en|Kamo shrines|WD=Q1306606|lt=Kamo Shrine}}Kitabatake Chikafusa, 『二十一社記』 賀茂社ノ条 or positing a deity of the {{ill|Izu Islands|en|Izu Islands|WD=Q864302|lt=Izu Islands}}.{{Cite book|和書|editor=|author=|year=1943|title=伊古奈比咩命神社|publisher=伊古奈比咩命神社|page=24|isbn=|ref=}} According to one interpretation, the Mishima deity of Iyo – originally venerated as Ōyamatsumi in Iyo – was combined through syncretism ({{ill|Religious syncretism|en|Religious syncretism|WD=Q21652002|lt=Syncretism}}) with the Watashi Ōkami from Settsu ({{ill|Settsu Province|en|Settsu Province|WD=Q864163|lt=Settsu}}) to form the Iyo Mishima deity. Another theory holds that the deity of the Izu Islands, regarded as Ōyamatsumi, after being transferred to the Mishima region later merged with a local water deity to form the Izu Mishima deity.日本の神社大全5 甲信/東海1 Among the representative descriptions found in pre‐medieval literature are the following: * In the 『Iyo Fudoki』 – the deity of Mishima (Mishima/Onshima) is identified as Ōyamatsumi. * In the {{ill|Engishiki Divine Name List|ja|延喜式神名帳|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki Divine Name List|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki Jinmyōchō|qq=}} – in Ochi District of Iyo Province, the great divine shrine “Ōyamatsumi Shrine” is listed (with Mishima Taisha appearing under the name “Izu Mishima Shrine”). * In {{ill|Tōkan Kikō|ja|東関紀行|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tōkan Kikō|1=Tōkan Kikō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11528660}}, {{ill|Genpei Jōsuiki|en|Genpei Jōsuiki|WD=Q3020148|lt=Genpei Seisui-ki}}, and {{ill|Shintōshū|en|Shintōshū|WD=Q2616931|lt=Shintōshū}} – the Izu Mishima deity is said to have come from Iyo. * In the 『Record of the Twenty-One Shrines』 and 『Deep Mountain Path in Spring』 – the Iyo and Izu Mishima deities are treated as identical. * In {{ill|Shaku Nihongi|en|Shaku Nihongi|WD=Q2710483|lt=Shaku Nihonki}}, {{ill|Nihon Shoki Sanso|ja|日本書紀纂疏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nihon Shoki Sanso|1=Nihon Shoki Sanso|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11508272}}, and {{ill|The Record of Japan's First Shrines|ja|大日本国一宮記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/The Record of Japan's First Shrines|1=Dai Nippon Koku Ichinomiya Ki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11435648}} – the Iyo and Izu Mishima deities are identified as Ōyamatsumi. * In the 『Record of the Twenty-Two Shrines Original Relations』 – the Iyo and Izu Mishima deities are identified as Kotoshironushi (this is cited as the basis for the Kotoshironushi theory; however, it is considered a misprint made during the transcription of the underlying 『Record of the Twenty-One Shrines』{{Cite book|和書|editor=|author=三島通良|year=1917|chapter=|title=伊豆国史蹟研究第一報書摘要|publisher=|isbn=|ref=}}). == History == For the founding legends of {{ill|Ōyamazumi Shrine|en|Ōyamazumi Shrine|WD=Q703904|lt=Ōyamazumi Shrine}} and {{ill|Mishima Taisha|en|Mishima Taisha|WD=Q650772|lt=Mishima Taisha}}, see their respective articles. Although both shrines have traditions of relocation (transference of the enshrined deity), both are generally negative about such transfers[https://oomishimagu.jp/about/ Ōyamatsumi Shrine – About][https://www.mishimataisha.or.jp/shrine Mishima Taisha History]. Excluding shrine legends, the earliest appearance of the deities in historical sources is found in the 『Shinshō Kakutoku Fushō』 (completed in 806), which records that in 758 the Izu Mishima deity was conferred a formal Rank. The 『Iyo Fudoki』 (believed to have been compiled by 748) also contains a passage stating that the deity of Mishima (Onshima) is Ōyamatsumi; however, the Fudoki itself has been lost and survives only as an excerpt quoted in the late Kamakura-period {{ill|Shaku Nihongi|en|Shaku Nihongi|WD=Q2710483|lt=Shaku Nihonki}}. The lost work 『Izu Kokufudoki』, too, contains no reference to the Izu Mishima deity in its scant surviving fragments. According to the 『Tango Kyūjiki』, it seems that the lost {{ill|Tango Kokufudoki|ja|丹後国風土記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tango Kokufudoki|1=Tango no Kuni Fudoki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11368517}} once mentioned {{ill|Mishimada Shrine|ja|三嶋田神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mishimada Shrine|1=Mishimada Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q131924351}}, but that work is also no longer extant. In other Heian-period sources, the place-name “Mishima” appears frequently – for example, it is first attested in {{ill|Wamyō Ruijushō|ja|倭名類聚抄|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wamyō Ruijushō|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 和名類聚抄}}. Several waka anthologies include poems about the Mishima deity; the Jitsukata-shū includes a poem on “mishima no kami”（Whether referring to Iyo or Settsu is unclear – 新日本古典文学大系）, and both the {{ill|Nōinshū|ja|能因集|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nōinshū|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} and {{ill|Kin'yō Wakashū|en|Kin'yō Wakashū|WD=Q1143249|lt=Konaha Wakashū}} contain poems about the Iyo Mishima deity (of Ōyamatsumi Shrine). The {{ill|Goshūi Wakashū|en|Goshūi Wakashū|WD=Q115108|lt=Goshūi Wakashū}} also includes a poem about the Eastern Journey ({{ill|Eastern Journey|ja|東遊|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Eastern Journey|1=Azuma Asobi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11528414}}) of the Iyo Mishima Myōjin. The tales of the Iyo Mishima deity are likewise recounted in the {{ill|Shunrai Zuinō|ja|俊頼髄脳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shunrai Zuinō|1=Toshiyori Zuinō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11385629}} and the {{ill|Ōkagami|en|Ōkagami|WD=Q385120|lt=Ōkagami}}. === Six Provinces History === In the Six Provinces History, three shrines are noted: Ōyamatsumi Shrine, Izu Mishima Shrine, and Mishima Kamo Shrine. Of these, the Ōyamatsumi Shrine of Iyo Province was successively promoted after being awarded the Junior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade (in {{ill|Shoku Nihongi|en|Shoku Nihongi|WD=Q611399|lt=Shoku Nihonki}}) in {{ill|766|en|766|WD=Q30564|lt=766}}, reaching the Senior Second Rank by 875 ({{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|en|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|WD=Q1052981|lt=The Three Generations of Japan: Official Records}}). The Izu Mishima deity is said to have manifested wondrous phenomena in 832, and as a result came to be regarded as a famous deity. However, the account in {{ill|Nihon Kōki|en|Nihon Kōki|WD=Q1077029|lt=Nihon Kōki}} (which covers the period 792–833) survives only in fragments quoted in {{ill|Shaku Nihongi|en|Shaku Nihongi|WD=Q2710483|lt=Shaku Nihonki}}, and it is presumed that a conferment of the Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade occurred around that time. In 850, the deity was awarded the Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade ({{ill|Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku|en|Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku|WD=Q1052905|lt=Nihon Buntoku Tennō Jitsuroku}}), and within a short period its divine Rank rapidly increased to the Junior Third Rank by 868 ({{ill|Ruijū Kokushi|en|Ruijū Kokushi|WD=Q1038639|lt=Ruiju Kokushi}}). In 884, the Mishima deity of Settsu Province was also awarded the Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade ({{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|en|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|WD=Q1052981|lt=The Three Generations of Japan: Official Records}}). After the period covered by the Six Provinces History, it is stated that Ōyamatsumi Shrine reached its Senior First Rank in {{ill|897|en|897|WD=Q30468|lt=897}}, and Izu Mishima Shrine reached the Senior First Rank by 1343, as recorded in the {{ill|Izu Province Divine Rank Register|ja|伊豆国神階帳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izu Province Divine Rank Register|1=Izu Province Divine Rank Register|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17193087}}. === Engishiki Divine Name List === The {{ill|Engishiki Divine Name List|ja|延喜式神名帳|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki Divine Name List|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki Jinmyōchō|qq=}}, completed in 927, records the following: * In Iyo Province’s Ochi District, the renowned divine shrine “Ōyamatsumi Shrine” (literally, “Ōyamatsumi Shrine”) – currently identified with the Ōyamatsumi Shrine of Daisan-shima. * In Izu Province’s Kamo District, the renowned divine shrine “Izu Mishima Shrine” – which is considered to be the predecessor of {{ill|Mishima Taisha|en|Mishima Taisha|WD=Q650772|lt=Mishima Taisha}}, though not identical; theories of transference or the enshrinement of a new shrine have been proposed. * In Echigo Province’s Kariwa District (displayed as “Mishima District”), the “Mishima Shrine” – which is regarded as the Mishima Shrine of Kashiwazaki City, though a transference theory exists.
(Here, {{ill|Kariwa District, Niigata|en|Kariwa District, Niigata|WD=Q1155110|lt=Mishima District}} is used to show the displayed name.) * In Tango Province’s Kumano District, the “Mishima-da Shrine” – currently represented by {{ill|Mishimada Shrine|ja|三嶋田神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mishimada Shrine|1=Mishimada Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q131924351}}. * In Settsu Province’s Shimogyo District, the “Mishima Kamo Shrine” – which is identified either with {{ill|Kamo Shrine (Takatsuki City)|ja|鴨神社 (高槻市)|lt=Kamo shrines|lt=Kamo Shrine|lt_ja=鴨神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamo Shrine (Takatsuki City)|1=Kamo Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11675604}} or with {{ill|Mishima Kamo Shrine|ja|三島鴨神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mishima Kamo Shrine|1=Mishima-Kamo Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11355295}}. In addition, a shrine known as Minishima Shrine in Takashima District of Ōmi Province – currently identified as {{ill|Minishima Shrine|ja|箕島神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Minishima Shrine|1=Mishima Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q134888252}} – is also considered to be part of the Mishima/Ōyamatsumi faith. == Shrines of Mishima and Ōyamatsumi Faith == When the principal shrine is taken to be the Ōyamatsumi Shrine of Daisan-shima ({{ill|Ōmishima Island|en|Ōmishima Island|WD=Q9009869|lt=Daisan-shima}}) and its Ōyamatsumi Shrine, the shrines are usually named “Mishima Shrine” or “Ōyamatsumi Shrine,” whereas when Mishima Taisha ({{ill|Mishima Taisha|en|Mishima Taisha|WD=Q650772|lt=Mishima Taisha}}) is regarded as the head shrine, the name “Mishima Shrine” is typically used. However, there are many exceptions and no fully systematized pattern. There are roughly 400 Mishima Shrines nationwide – approximately 111 in Ehime Prefecture and 36 in {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|en|Shizuoka Prefecture|WD=Q131320|lt=Shizuoka Prefecture}}, among others. Similarly, Ōyamatsumi Shrines are said to number between 293 and 897『大三島宮』1973rd year 1月。大三島大社講, or even up to 960, with 43 in {{ill|Fukuoka Prefecture|en|Fukuoka Prefecture|WD=Q123258|lt=Fukuoka Prefecture}} and 36 in {{ill|Fukushima Prefecture|en|Fukushima Prefecture|WD=Q71707|lt=Fukushima Prefecture}}, among others. Other related shrine names include Yama Shrines, numbering 78 (in {{ill|Kōchi Prefecture|en|Kōchi Prefecture|WD=Q134093|lt=Kōchi Prefecture}}, {{ill|Nagasaki Prefecture|en|Nagasaki Prefecture|WD=Q169376|lt=Nagasaki Prefecture}}, Fukuoka Prefecture, etc.), and Ōyama Shrines, numbering 42 (in {{ill|Hiroshima Prefecture|en|Hiroshima Prefecture|WD=Q617375|lt=Hiroshima Prefecture}}, Kōchi Prefecture, {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|en|Shimane Prefecture|WD=Q132751|lt=Shimane Prefecture}}, etc.), as well as Yamazumi Shrines, with 7 in (for example, {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|en|Shizuoka Prefecture|WD=Q131320|lt=Shizuoka Prefecture}}, etc.). In addition to these, shrines where Ōyamatsumi is the principal enshrined deity include, for example, the {{ill|Yama Shrine|ja|山神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yama Shrine|1=Mountain Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11470798}} (numbering 1,133), among others. Furthermore, when including subsidiary halls and sub-shrines within the precincts, the total number of shrines that enshrine Ōyamatsumi in some form is said to reach between 7,000[https://kaken.nii.ac.jp/ja/report/KAKENHI-PROJECT-17K02270/17K022702019jisseki/ 祭神別神社分布図による諸信仰伝播の過程および背景の研究（2019th year ）] and 10,0001973rd year 1月『大三島宮』大三島大社講（大山祇神社）1972nd year 8月の神社本庁調査に依る, and these are, at least in formal terms, sometimes regarded as subordinate to the head shrine, Ōyamatsumi Shrine of Daisan-shima[https://kojiki.kokugakuin.ac.jp/shinmei/oyamatsuminokami/ 大山津見神](國學院大學神名データベース). However, this relationship is a formal one based solely on the enshrined deities; the actual connection to the Mishima/Ōyamatsumi faith varies considerably – for example, the group of 438 shrines that enshrine Ōyamatsumi as one of twelve deities (the “Twelve-Shrine Faith”) is only loosely related, whereas the faith centered on the Asama Shrine (397 shrines), which frequently distributes Ōyamatsumi, is based on a parent–child relationship between the Mishima and Asama deities権 東祐「神話解釈史から見る富士山の祭神変貌論」『日本研究』（2023rd year 12月16日) {{doi|10.15055/00006788}}. === Major Shrines === ;Headquarters * [[ja:三島・大山祇信仰]] [[ja:三島・大山祇信仰]] [[ja:三島・大山祇信仰]] [[File:Ohyamazumi Shrine Haiden.JPG|270px|thumb|[[Ōyamazumi Shrine]]]] [[File:Mishima-taisha shaden.JPG|270px|thumb|[[Mishima Taisha]]]] The Mishima and Ōyamazumi faith ('''三島・大山祇信仰) is a Shinto faith centered on the two shrines [[Ōyamazumi Shrine]] and [[Mishima Taisha]] {{Cite book|和書|author=岡田莊司・加藤直弥|date=2007|publisher=國學院大|title=現代・神社の信仰分布|isbn=|pages=25-27}}'''. == Overview == This group of shrines is primarily represented by those called {{ill|Mishima Taisha|lt=Mishima Taisha|lt=Mishima Shrine|ja|三島神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mishima Shrine|qq=}} (also written as 三嶋神社) and {{ill|Ōyamazumi Shrine|en|Ōyamazumi Shrine|WD=Q703904|lt=Ōyamazumi Shrine|1=Ōyamazumi Shrine}} (also written as 大山積神社). There are approximately 700 to 1,300Ōmishima Town History, "Ōyamazumi Shrine Edition" shrines with these names across Japan. They exist in 44 {{ill|Prefectures of Japan|en|Prefectures of Japan|WD=Q50337|lt=prefectures of Japan|1=Prefectures of Japan}}, ranging from {{ill|Hokkaido|en|Hokkaido|WD=Q35581|lt=Hokkaidō|1=Hokkaido}} to {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture|1=Kagoshima Prefecture}}, though the densest concentration of worship is observed from {{ill|Western Shikoku|ja|西四国|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Western Shikoku|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 四国|1=Shikoku|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q13991}} to {{ill|Kyushu|en|Kyushu|WD=Q13987|lt=Kyūshū|1=Kyushu}}, as well as the periphery of the {{ill|Kantō region|en|Kantō region|WD=Q132480|lt=Kantō region|1=Kantō region}}, particularly in {{ill|Fukushima Prefecture|en|Fukushima Prefecture|WD=Q71707|lt=Fukushima Prefecture|1=Fukushima Prefecture}}, {{ill|Niigata Prefecture|en|Niigata Prefecture|WD=Q132705|lt=Niigata Prefecture|1=Niigata Prefecture}}, and {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|en|Shizuoka Prefecture|WD=Q131320|lt=Shizuoka Prefecture|1=Shizuoka Prefecture}}. In {{ill|Ehime Prefecture|en|Ehime Prefecture|WD=Q123376|lt=Ehime Prefecture|1=Ehime Prefecture}}, where the Ōyamazumi Shrine on Ōmishima Island is located, the shrines are particularly concentrated, with over 100 Mishima Shrines alone. Within the prefecture, it is the most commonly worshiped shrine lineage{{Cite book |和書 |author=岡田莊司・加藤直弥 |date=2007 |publisher=國學院大 |title=現代・神社の信仰分布 |isbn= |pages=60 }}. Other regions with significant numbers include {{ill|Fukuoka Prefecture|en|Fukuoka Prefecture|WD=Q123258|lt=Fukuoka Prefecture|1=Fukuoka Prefecture}} and {{ill|Kōchi Prefecture|en|Kōchi Prefecture|WD=Q134093|lt=Kōchi Prefecture|1=Kōchi Prefecture}}. The {{ill|Ōyamatsumi|en|Ōyamatsumi|WD=Q386563|WD=Q386563|lt=Ōyamatsumi|1=Ōyamatsumi}} deity, historically regarded as a Mishima deity, was originally a god of mountains. However, since Ōyamazumi Shrine is situated on the island of {{ill|Ōmishima Island|en|Ōmishima Island|WD=Q9009869|lt=Ōmishima|1=Ōmishima Island}}, and {{ill|Mishima Taisha|en|Mishima Taisha|WD=Q650772|lt=Mishima Taisha|1=Mishima Taisha}} was once believed to have been located in the {{ill|Izu Islands|en|Izu Islands|WD=Q864302|lt=Izu Islands|1=Izu Islands}}, the Mishima deity has strong associations with maritime protection and island creation. From the mid-{{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, the shrine gained the reverence of the {{ill|Kōno clan|ja|河野氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōno clan|qq=}} and the {{ill|Minamoto clan|en|Minamoto clan|WD=Q599881|lt=Genji|1=Minamoto clan}}, among other warrior families, and became well known as a god of war. The {{ill|Azuma Kagami|en|Azuma Kagami|WD=Q1042324|lt=Azuma Kagami|1=Azuma Kagami}} records that {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|en|Minamoto no Yoritomo|WD=Q242800|lt=Minamoto no Yoritomo|1=Minamoto no Yoritomo}} prayed at Mishima Taisha before raising his army‘Azuma Kagami’, Jishō 4 (治承四年) August 17. Additionally, 40% of the {{ill|National Treasure (Japan)|en|National Treasure (Japan)|WD=Q1139795|lt=National Treasures of Japan|1=National Treasure (Japan)}} and {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|en|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|WD=Q1188622|lt=Important Cultural Property|1=Important Cultural Property (Japan)}} classified as weapons and armor are housed at the Ōyamazumi Shrine on Ōmishima. The deity was also worshipped as an agricultural god, with many records of rainmaking rituals. The Mishima Shrines across Japan can generally be classified into two major lineages based on their origin: the Iyo lineage and the Izu lineage. However, the categorization is not rigid, as some shrines have ancient origins, others claim descent from both lineages, and some perceive both shrines as the same deity. Until the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji period|1=Meiji era}}, Mishima Taisha was considered to be derived from the Ōyamazumi Shrine on Ōmishima, and they mutually influenced each other. The {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period|1=Kamakura period}} text *Haruno no Miyamaji* (春の深山路) describes both shrines as regarding each other as their main shrine*Haruno no Miyamaji*, November 24. As of 2023, Ōyamazumi Shrine on Ōmishima enshrines {{ill|Ōyamazumi|ja|大山積神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōyamazumi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to オオヤマツミ|1=Ōyamatsumi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q386563}}[http://ehime-jinjacho.jp/jinja/?p=1542 Ehime Prefecture Shrine Association - Ōyamazumi Shrine], while Mishima Taisha, after undergoing another change in enshrined deities, now venerates both Ōyamazumi and {{ill|Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|WD=Q8009611|lt=Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|WD=Q8009611|lt=Kotoshironushi|ja|事代主神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotoshironushi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 事代主|1=Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto}}, collectively worshiped as {{ill|Mishima Daimyōjin|ja|三島大明神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mishima Daimyōjin|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 三島・大山祇信仰|1=Mishima–Ōyamazumi cult|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q127948103}} or the Mishima deity[https://www.mishimataisha.or.jp/shrine Mishima Taisha Official Site]. == Worshipped Deities (Saijin) == {{see also|{{ill|Saijin|ja|祭神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saijin|qq=}}}} The current {{ill|Enshrined Deities|ja|祭神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Enshrined Deities|1=Saijin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11591100}} are as follows: at Daisan‐shima’s Ōyamatsumi Shrine, the deity {{ill|Ōyamatsumi|en|Ōyamatsumi|WD=Q386563|WD=Q386563|lt=Ōyamatsumi|1=Ōyamatsumi}}; at Mishima Taisha, the deities are Ōyamatsumi (大山祇命) and {{ill|Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|WD=Q8009611|lt=Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|WD=Q8009611|lt=Kotoshironushi|ja|事代主神|WD=Q8009611|lt=Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|WD=Q8009611|lt=Kotoshironushi|lt_ja=積羽八重事代主神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotoshironushi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 事代主|1=Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto}}. In Ōyamatsumi Shrines such as {{ill|Ōyamatsumi Shrine (disambiguation)|ja|大山祇神社 (曖昧さ回避)|WD=Q386563|lt=Ōyamatsumi Shrine|lt_ja=大山祇神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōyamatsumi Shrine (disambiguation)|1=Ōyamatsumi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q16278443}} and in the Iyo lineage of Mishima Shrines the deity Ōyamatsumi is venerated, while in the Izu lineage of Mishima Shrines either Ōyamatsumi or Kotoshironushi is enshrined singly or both are enshrined together. Besides the names Ōyamatsumi (命) and Ōyamatsumi (命), variants such as Ōyamatsumi Tsumi, Ōyamatsumi Sumino, and Ōyamatsumi Tsutsumi are also attested. In both Mishima Taisha and the Izu lineage of Mishima Shrines, it is recorded that before the Edo period the enshrined deity was Ōyamatsumi (命), and it was only after the Meiji period that Kotoshironushi came to be enshrined. This change has not been without criticism{{Cite book|和書|editor=教部省|author=|year=1925|title={{ill|Selected Divine Names List|ja|特選神名牒|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Selected Divine Names List|1=Tokusen Jinmyōchō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11571092}}|publisher=磯部甲陽堂|page=299p|isbn=|ref=}}; at Mishima Taisha, in {{ill|1952|en|1952|WD=Q5272|lt=1952|1=1952}}, the two deities Ōyamatsumi and Kotoshironushi were collectively re-designated and enshrined as either “Mishima Daimyōjin” or “Mishima Shrine.” For details on the post-Meiji changes in the enshrined deities at Mishima Taisha, see {{ill|Mishima Taisha#About the enshrined deities|ja|三嶋大社#祭神について|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mishima Taisha#About the enshrined deities|qq=}}. There are various theories regarding the identity of the Mishima deity. In addition to the Ōyamatsumi theory and the Kotoshironushi theory, there exist theories equating this deity with that of {{ill|Kamo shrines|en|Kamo shrines|WD=Q1306606|lt=Kamo Shrine|1=Kamo shrines}}Kitabatake Chikafusa, 『二十一社記』 賀茂社ノ条 or positing a deity of the {{ill|Izu Islands|en|Izu Islands|WD=Q864302|lt=Izu Islands|1=Izu Islands}}.{{Cite book|和書|editor=|author=|year=1943|title=伊古奈比咩命神社|publisher=伊古奈比咩命神社|page=24|isbn=|ref=}} According to one interpretation, the Mishima deity of Iyo – originally venerated as Ōyamatsumi in Iyo – was combined through syncretism ({{ill|Religious syncretism|en|Religious syncretism|WD=Q21652002|lt=Syncretism|1=Religious syncretism}}) with the Watashi Ōkami from Settsu ({{ill|Settsu Province|en|Settsu Province|WD=Q864163|lt=Settsu|1=Settsu Province}}) to form the Iyo Mishima deity. Another theory holds that the deity of the Izu Islands, regarded as Ōyamatsumi, after being transferred to the Mishima region later merged with a local water deity to form the Izu Mishima deity.日本の神社大全5 甲信/東海1 Among the representative descriptions found in pre‐medieval literature are the following: * In the 『Iyo Fudoki』 – the deity of Mishima (Mishima/Onshima) is identified as Ōyamatsumi. * In the {{ill|Engishiki Divine Name List|ja|延喜式神名帳|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki {{ill|Shintōshū|en|Shintōshū|WD=Q2616931|lt=Shintōshū|1=Shintōshū}} – the Izu Mishima deity is said to have come from Iyo. * In the 『Record of the Twenty-One Shrines』 and 『Deep Mountain Path in Sanso|ja|日本書紀纂疏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nihon Shoki Sanso|1=Nihon Shoki Sanso|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11508272}}, and {{ill|The Record of Japan's First Shrines|ja|大日本国一宮記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/The Record of Japan's First Shrines|1=Dai Nippon Koku Ichinomiya Ki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11435648}} – the Iyo and Izu Mishima
